toc.title: Your nervous system knows the truth

blocks.p: Have you ever left a therapy session feeling worse than when you walked in?
Maybe you felt triggered, dysregulated, or even retraumatized. You might have wondered: "Is this normal? Should therapy hurt like this?"
The answer is complicated, and understanding why is essential for benefitting from therapy, coaching, or other 1-on-1 self-development options.
Therapy should be a safe space to work through the obstacles holding you back. But sometimes, despite a therapist's best intentions, therapy can inadvertently retraumatize you.
Other times, it's due to the therapist's unethical behavior.

Retraumatization happens when something triggers your nervous system back into a defensive state similar to, or even more intense than, the original trauma. In therapy, this is especially concerning because you've sought out a safe space to heal, and instead, you leave dysregulated and more stuck than before.
This shouldn't happen. But it does. And not always because your therapist is unethical.

Sometimes retraumatization occurs because of a common misunderstanding in the field: the belief that clients need to confront and relive their trauma in detail before they can heal from it. Other times, it is indeed due to unethical behavior, like when a therapist exploits the power dynamic inherent in the therapeutic relationship.
Let me walk you through both.

blocks.h: Two paths to retraumatization in therapy

blocks.p: The first path involves unethical behavior. The second involves a well-intentioned but potentially harmful therapeutic approach. Understanding the difference matters.

blocks.h3: Path #1: unethical therapist behavior (the power imbalance problem)

blocks.p: Therapy can go seriously wrong when a therapist acts outside the profession's ethical norms, laws, and standards.

This might look extreme: manipulating a client into a sexual relationship ([therapy never includes sex](https://www.dca.ca.gov/publications/proftherapy.shtml)), exploiting financial dependency, or weaponizing the therapeutic relationship for personal gain. But it can also be subtler, a therapist who maintains unnecessary power over a client, who dismisses their concerns, or who uses their position of authority to control.

The core issue is this: therapy inherently involves a power imbalance. You're seeking help. Your therapist is positioned as the expert. This dynamic, when handled ethically, is collaborative and has healthy boundaries. But when a therapist has ill intent, it becomes a setup for exploitation.

If you have a history of poor attachment or if you live stuck lower on your Polyvagal ladder (in fight, flight, freeze, or [shutdown states](piece:dorsal-vagal-shutdown)), you may struggle to identify red flags. You might not notice when a boundary is crossed. This is normal for someone stuck in a defensive state; they miss others' interpersonal cues of danger.

And in a relationship with an inherent power imbalance that relies on vulnerability and trust but is really a one-way relationship, that defensive state of vulnerability of missing danger cues can be exploited even more easily.

Much of how therapy is taught reinforces this power dynamic. The therapist is positioned as the "expert" who identifies the problem, labels it, and then dispenses a remedy. The client is the problem-haver, the one seeking the fix. This medical model has limited usefulness and, frankly, can enable exploitation.

Ethical therapy should be different. It should be collaborative. Two individuals meeting, each bringing their expertise: the therapist's in psychology and technique, and the client's in their own life. The therapist and the client work together toward a shared goal.

When a therapist steps outside this collaborative stance, when they use their position of authority to manipulate, control, or exploit, that's not therapy anymore. It's [a therapist behaving badly](https://youtu.be/V-hzwyxp4E0). And it's retraumatizing.

blocks.h3: Path #2: premature trauma work (the common therapeutic mistake)

blocks.p: Here's where things get more nuanced. Retraumatization can happen even when a therapist is doing their best.

We're commonly taught in therapy schools that to "heal" from trauma, clients need to talk about it, directly, in detail, and with emotional intensity. They need to confront their feelings. Process it all. Feel it fully. Release it cathartically.

Whole therapeutic modalities are built on this idea, like [Trauma-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/therapy-types/trauma-focused-cognitive-behavior-therapy) (TF-CBT) and [EMDR](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/therapy-types/emdr).

These modalities are not, in and of themselves, retraumatizing, as they include built-in management features, bilateral stimulation, working with a trusted caregiver, gradual exposure, and structured pacing. They can be effective when implemented skillfully, with the therapist's co-regulation, and with a client's full informed consent.
(Although I have heard many, many therapy and coaching clients tell me that when they went through Trauma-Focused CBT and EMDR, they checked out. They went numb. They shut down.)

Therapists, no matter what modality they use, run the risk of retraumatizing their clients, maybe especially from modalities that require the client to tell the trauma narrative. But besides that, many therapists operate from a pervasive belief that clients need to confront and share their trauma narratives regardless of readiness, or without assessing client readiness.

These therapists believe clients need to "feel their feelings" before they know the client is ready. That clients need to "sit with" their difficult emotions, even without knowing if they lack the biological capacity to do so safely.

blocks.h: What actually happens: the defensive state trap

blocks.p: When a therapist pushes a client into trauma work before they're ready, no matter their modality and before the client has access to their Polyvagal state of safety, the nervous system does what it was designed to do: it defends.

The client becomes triggered back into fight, flight, freeze, or shutdown. They're no longer in the therapy session, safely and intentionally processing past events. They're back in the moment of the trauma itself, without the capacity to self-regulate. They leave the session dysregulated and retraumatized. Their stuck autonomic nervous system state is simply reinforced.

The therapist may not realize they're doing this. They might even believe they're doing excellent work. "Look," they think, "I got my client to confront their past. I got them to feel their feelings. I got them to sit with difficult emotions. That's good therapy, right?"
No, that's not necessarily good therapy.

All of these things, confronting, feeling, sitting with difficult emotions, can be deeply healing. But only when the client is ready. Only when their nervous system has the capacity to process these experiences without tipping into dysregulation.

blocks.h: Why safety comes first: the Polyvagal perspective

blocks.p: The "vagal brake" is a Polyvagal Theory concept. [New to the Polyvagal Theory? Start here.](piece:snb101-polyvagal-101-foundations)

Your ventral vagal pathways, the myelinated vagal fibers responsible for social connection and all the wonderful positive feelings we want more of, act like a brake on your defensive sympathetic nervous system. When these pathways are active and strong, your heart rate stays calmer. Your flight/fight responses stay at a manageable level. You can access connection, presence, and the capacity to process difficult experiences.

When these pathways are weak or offline, when you don't have access to your [Polyvagal safety state](piece:polyvagal-safety), your heart rate climbs. Your sympathetic nervous system kicks in. You experience anxiety, panic, overwhelm, and uncontrollable anger. Your body is in a state of defense.

This is one possibility of what happens in premature trauma work. The therapist asks the client to revisit their trauma before the vagal brake is strong. The safety pathways go offline. The sympathetic system floods. Dysregulation follows.
Or, if the client is in a [shutdown state](hub:shutdown), they simply continue to shut down, losing access to any safety in their system.
The solution is clear: safety comes first.

blocks.h: The right way to do trauma work: safety first, then integration

blocks.p: Effective trauma recovery follows a specific sequence:
First, build access to your Polyvagal safety state. This means strengthening your ventral vagal pathways through simple daily practices that activate a sense of connection.
These are three beginner-level homework assignments to practice feeling connection, appropriate for any client:

ol: Take one extended exhale once a day.
Spend 30 seconds mindfully focused on one sense.
Step outside once a day to feel the air on your skin.

blocks.why: Thirty seconds with one sense, an exhale, the air on your skin: simple mindfulness builds the safety that comes first.

blocks.p: Safety is foundational work. It's not optional.
As you practice safety through even simple methods, you will gradually strengthen your safety state. This creates a higher Safety Baseline, with benefits across all areas of your life.

In a therapy session, you want a higher continuous Safety Baseline and a higher Safety Moment. We want a sufficiently high level of safety in this particular therapeutic Moment to turn our attention to non-safety.
These are three simple ways to identify if you have a strong enough anchoring in safety in a specific Safety Moment:

ol: Ability to connect with the senses mindfully
Curiosity or interest in non-safety experiences

blocks.p: You can learn more about Safety Moments and Baseline in [Stuck Not Broken: Book 2](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/books).

Once you're anchored in safety, truly anchored, not just intellectually understanding it, then you can turn your attention toward the more difficult experiences. Then you can explore your grief, shame, and trauma.

But even as you do this deeper work, you're continuously checking in with yourself: Am I still anchored? Do I still have access to my safety state? Can I continue, or do I need to pause and re-regulate?

It's completely normal and expected that defensive energies surface during trauma work. They will come up. Fight, flight, freeze, shutdown, these states will emerge as you begin to process what's been stuck in your body.
But they shouldn't overwhelm you. They shouldn't dysregulate you because you're balancing them with access to safety.

You're feeling the stuck fight/flight, but you're also feeling calm and possibility. You're touching into shutdown, but you're also connected and present. You're processing the freeze while also grounded and resourced.
This is what safety-first and Polyvagal-informed trauma work looks like.

blocks.h: How to know if your therapy is retraumatizing: red flags to watch for

blocks.p: Sometimes you won't know until you're in it. But here are signs that your therapy experience may be retraumatizing:

ul: You leave sessions feeling more dysregulated than when you arrived, not the temporary intensity of processing, but actual dysregulation with no sense of return to calm. Dysregulation shows up as flashbacks, intrusive thoughts, panic, overwhelm, rage, and fear.
Your therapist pushes you to discuss trauma before you feel ready, dismissing your hesitations as avoidance rather than wisdom.

Your therapist positions themselves as the "expert dispensing a remedy" rather than collaborating with you as an equal partner in your trauma recovery. There's a noticeable power imbalance that doesn't feel safe, where your concerns are dismissed or minimized. They may respond defensively when you ask about the process.
You're discussing traumatic events without any grounding techniques or safety resources offered.

blocks.p: If you're experiencing any of these, it may be time to have a direct conversation with your therapist about your concerns. If they respond defensively or dismissively, it may be time to seek a different therapeutic relationship. Your nervous system's signal that something isn't safe deserves to be honored, not pathologized.

blocks.h: Frequently asked questions: therapy, safety, and retraumatization

blocks.h3: How do I know if I'm avoiding trauma work vs. my nervous system telling me I'm not ready?

blocks.p: Great question. Your nervous system's wisdom and avoidance can feel similar, but they're different.
Avoidance often includes shame, self-judgment, or stories like "I should be over this by now." It's the mind trying to protect you through distraction or denial.

Nervous system wisdom feels quieter. It's a sense of "not yet" or "I need support first." You might feel curious about the work, but your body signals that you need more grounding. This is not avoidance, it's your biology being honest about your current capacity.
The key: Listen to your body's signals without judgment. If your body says "not yet," that's valuable information. A good therapist will respect this and work with you to build safety first.

blocks.prompt: Is there something your body is saying "not yet" to? What does that "not yet" feel like?

blocks.h3: What if my therapist dismisses my concerns about the pace or process?

blocks.p: This is a red flag.

In ethical, collaborative therapy, your concerns about the process are the process. If your therapist dismisses your hesitations, responds defensively, or makes you feel bad for speaking up, that's not a safe therapeutic relationship.
You have options:

ol: Have a direct conversation: "I'm noticing I feel dysregulated after sessions. I'd like to slow down and focus on safety first. What do you think?"
If they respond defensively: trust that signal. You may need a different therapist.
If you're unsure: seek a second opinion from another trauma-informed therapist. Yes, this is okay to do, though continuing with two therapists is not a great idea, typically.

blocks.p: Your comfort with the pace is not negotiable. A good therapist wants to hear this.

blocks.h3: I've already experienced retraumatization in therapy. What do I do now?

blocks.p: First: you're not broken, and seeking help again takes courage.
Right now:

ul: Give yourself grace. Your nervous system was trying to protect you.
Find a trauma-informed therapist who understands Polyvagal Theory or at least prioritizes safety-first approaches.
Before starting therapy with someone new, ask them directly: "How do you approach building safety before diving into trauma work?"

blocks.p: Moving forward:

ul: Prioritize building your Safety Baseline through simple, small daily practices (extended exhales, mindful sensory focus, time outside).
Work with someone who understands that healing isn't about forcing yourself to feel or remember, it's about gradually building the capacity to feel safe while processing what's stuck.

blocks.p: Healing after retraumatization is absolutely possible. It just needs to happen at the right pace, in the right way.

blocks.h3: Are certain therapy modalities safer than others?

blocks.p: This is a nuanced question.

Modalities like TF-CBT and EMDR aren't inherently retraumatizing, they have built-in safety features. But they can be retraumatizing if implemented before a client has a strong safety baseline, or if the therapist isn't checking in on the client's capacity throughout.
What matters more than the modality is:

ul: Does your therapist prioritize your safety baseline before diving into trauma?
Do they check in with you about your capacity to continue?
Do they offer grounding techniques during difficult work?
Are they collaborative, or do they position themselves as the expert "fixing" you?

blocks.p: A skilled, trauma-informed therapist using almost any modality will be safer than an unskilled therapist using a "safe" modality. The implementation matters more than the name.

blocks.h3: How long does it take to build a strong enough safety baseline for trauma work?

blocks.p: It depends on your history and starting point. There's no timeline.
For someone with a relatively stable nervous system, consistent, small safety practices can strengthen their baseline in weeks.

For someone with Complex PTSD or chronic shutdown, this process is slower and more nuanced. It's about gradually building tolerance to safety in small doses, like gradually increasing weight in physical training.

Absolutely, I do. I work with my clients to identify safety, build it, and maintain it. A ton of progress can come from this. If the client wants to, we can venture into trauma narratives, but I typically don't do this. However, it's very common to guide clients through navigating their defensive activation while anchored in safety.
I find that if clients can mindfully connect with their defense, they don't need to tell me their trauma narratives.

blocks.h: Your nervous system knows the truth

blocks.p: Retraumatization in therapy is a real risk. But it's not inevitable. Understanding how it happens, whether through unethical behavior or premature trauma work, empowers you to protect yourself.

Remember this: your nervous system's protective response isn't a sign that you're broken or that you should push harder. It's information. It's wisdom. When your body signals that something isn't safe, that's your biology protecting you. And that protection deserves respect.

If your therapy experience has been retraumatizing, healing is still possible. You're not broken. Your nervous system is doing precisely what it was designed to do. The next step is finding a trauma-informed, safety-first approach that honors your biology and supports your genuine recovery.

ul: You're not broken; your biology is protecting you.
Retraumatization in therapy can result from either unethical therapist behavior (exploitation) or therapeutic approaches that push trauma work before safety is established.
Effective therapy should be collaborative, not hierarchical. The therapist brings expertise in technique; you bring expertise in your life.
The Polyvagal safety state must be established and strengthened before engaging in deeper trauma work.
When your nervous system signals that something isn't safe in therapy, that's valuable information, not resistance to overcome.
Safety-first trauma work means balancing the processing of stuck defensive states with continuous access to your Polyvagal safety state.
If your therapy feels retraumatizing, you deserve a different approach. Your signals matter.
